questions.question: Which of the following is a scalar quantity?
questions.explanation: Energy has only magnitude and a unit (joule); it has no direction associated with it. The other three are vectors.

questions.question: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explanation: Acceleration is a change in velocity per unit time — both magnitude and direction matter, so it is a vector. Mass, temperature and time are scalars.

questions.question: Which pair lists ONE scalar and ONE vector?
questions.explanation: Speed is a scalar (magnitude only), velocity is a vector (magnitude + direction). Force and momentum are both vectors; displacement and acceleration are both vectors; mass and energy are both scalars.

questions.question: The magnitude of a unit vector is
questions.explanation: By definition a unit vector has magnitude exactly 1 and is used purely to indicate direction.

questions.question: Two vectors are said to be equal when
options: their magnitudes are equal, irrespective of direction
their directions are the same, irrespective of magnitude
both their magnitudes and directions are equal
they start from the same point
questions.answer: both their magnitudes and directions are equal
questions.explanation: A vector is fully specified by magnitude and direction. Two vectors are equal only if both agree; their position on the page is irrelevant.

questions.question: A vector can be slid parallel to itself anywhere on the page without changing it. This is because
options: a vector has no fixed point of application — only magnitude and direction matter
questions.answer: a vector has no fixed point of application — only magnitude and direction matter
questions.explanation: A free vector is specified by its magnitude and direction alone; its location on the page is just a drawing convenience.

questions.question: The unit vector î points along which axis?
questions.explanation: Standard convention: î along x, ĵ along y, k̂ along z.

questions.question: A 2D vector A in component form is written as
questions.explanation: The components are signed scalars multiplying the unit vectors along the chosen axes.

questions.question: The triangle law of vector addition states that if two vectors are represented in magnitude and direction by two sides of a triangle taken in order, their resultant is represented by
options: the third side taken in the same order
the third side taken in the opposite order
the longest side of the triangle
questions.answer: the third side taken in the opposite order
questions.explanation: Taken in opposite order: tail of A → head of B is the same as the third side of the triangle drawn in reverse, which represents the resultant R = A + B.

questions.question: Two vectors of magnitudes 3 and 4 act at right angles. The magnitude of their resultant is
questions.explanation: R = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5. (From R² = A² + B² + 2AB cos 90° with cos 90° = 0.)

questions.question: Two equal vectors of magnitude A act at an angle of 60°. The magnitude of their resultant is
questions.explanation: R² = A² + A² + 2A² cos 60° = 2A² + 2A²(1/2) = 3A², so R = A√3.

questions.question: Two equal vectors of magnitude A act at an angle of 120°. The magnitude of their resultant is
questions.explanation: R² = A² + A² + 2A²(−1/2) = A², so R = A.

questions.question: The maximum value of the resultant of two vectors A and B (with magnitudes A and B) is
questions.explanation: Maximum when the vectors are parallel (θ = 0); R² = A² + B² + 2AB = (A + B)², so R = A + B.

questions.question: The minimum value of the resultant of two vectors of magnitudes A and B (A > B) is
questions.explanation: Minimum when the vectors are anti-parallel (θ = 180°); R² = A² + B² − 2AB = (A − B)², so R = |A − B|.

questions.question: Two vectors of magnitudes 5 N and 12 N can have a resultant whose magnitude could NOT possibly be
questions.explanation: The resultant lies between |A − B| = 7 and A + B = 17. So 7, 13, 17 are all possible; 20 is outside the range.

questions.question: A vector of magnitude 10 makes an angle of 30° with the x-axis. Its x-component is
A vector of magnitude 10 makes an angle of 30° with the x-axis. Its y-component is
If A = 3î + 4ĵ, then the magnitude of A is
If A = 3î + 4ĵ, the angle A makes with the x-axis is approximately
questions.explanation: tan θ = A_y / A_x = 4/3, so θ = arctan(4/3) ≈ 53°.

questions.question: If A = 2î + 3ĵ and B = î − 2ĵ, then A + B equals
questions.explanation: Add components: x = 2 + 1 = 3, y = 3 + (−2) = 1. So A + B = 3î + ĵ.

questions.question: If A = 4î + 3ĵ and B = î + ĵ, then A − B equals
questions.explanation: Subtract components: (4 − 1)î + (3 − 1)ĵ = 3î + 2ĵ.

questions.question: Three forces of equal magnitude act at a point such that their resultant is zero. The angle between any two of them is
questions.explanation: Three equal coplanar vectors sum to zero only if they are arranged symmetrically at 120° to each other (think of vertices of an equilateral triangle).

questions.question: Two vectors of magnitudes 4 and 5 give a resultant of magnitude √61. The angle between them is
For a particle moving in a plane with constant acceleration, the x- and y-components of motion are
options: coupled and must be solved together
independent, each obeying the 1D kinematic equations
questions.answer: independent, each obeying the 1D kinematic equations
questions.explanation: When a is constant, the kinematic equations apply to each component separately; they share only the time variable t.

questions.question: If r(t) = x(t) î + y(t) ĵ, the velocity is
questions.explanation: Velocity is the time derivative of position. Each component is differentiated independently.

questions.question: In 2D motion with constant acceleration, the x- and y- motions are linked only by
questions.explanation: Each component obeys its own 1D equations; the only shared quantity is the elapsed time.

questions.question: A particle starts from origin with velocity (3î + 4ĵ) m/s and has constant acceleration (−î) m/s². Its velocity after 2 s is
questions.explanation: Apply v = u + at component-wise: v_x = 3 + (−1)(2) = 1; v_y = 4 + 0 = 4.

questions.question: A particle has initial velocity (2î + 3ĵ) m/s and acceleration (0.5î + ĵ) m/s². Its velocity at t = 4 s is
The path of a projectile (in the absence of air resistance) is
questions.explanation: y is quadratic in x in the projectile path equation y = x tan θ − g x² / (2 u² cos² θ), which is the equation of a parabola.

questions.question: The horizontal velocity of a projectile (no air resistance) during flight
questions.explanation: There is no horizontal force, so a_x = 0 and v_x = u cos θ throughout the flight.

questions.question: At the highest point of its trajectory, a projectile has
questions.explanation: The vertical velocity is zero at the apex (it reverses there). The horizontal velocity u cos θ persists.

questions.question: The acceleration of a projectile during its flight (no air resistance) is
options: u, directed along the launch direction
questions.explanation: Gravity is the only force acting, producing acceleration g vertically downward throughout the flight.

questions.question: A projectile is launched at speed 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Its initial vertical velocity is (take g = 10 m/s²)
A projectile is launched at speed 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Its horizontal velocity component is
A projectile launched at 20 m/s at 30° has a time of flight of (g = 10 m/s²)
A projectile launched at 20 m/s at 30° reaches a maximum height of (g = 10 m/s²)
A projectile launched at 20 m/s at 30° has a range of (g = 10 m/s²)
The range of a projectile on level ground is maximum when the launch angle is
questions.explanation: R = u² sin 2θ / g; sin 2θ is maximum (=1) when 2θ = 90°, i.e. θ = 45°.

questions.question: Two projectiles are launched at the same speed with angles 30° and 60° on level ground. Their ranges are
questions.explanation: Complementary angles (θ + 90° − θ = 90°) give the same range because sin 2(60°) = sin 120° = sin 60° = sin 2(30°).

questions.question: Of two projectiles launched at 30° and 60° at the same speed, which has the greater maximum height?
questions.explanation: H = u² sin² θ / (2g). sin² 60° > sin² 30°, so the 60° projectile rises higher.

questions.question: If the speed of a projectile is doubled (same angle), the range becomes
questions.explanation: R ∝ u² (with θ fixed). Doubling u multiplies the range by 4.

questions.question: If g were suddenly halved (other things being equal), the range of a projectile would
questions.explanation: R = u² sin 2θ / g, so R ∝ 1/g. Halving g doubles the range.

questions.question: A stone is thrown horizontally from a 45-m high tower at 10 m/s. The time it takes to reach the ground is (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Vertical free fall from rest: h = (1/2) g t², so 45 = 5 t², t² = 9, t = 3 s.

questions.question: A stone is thrown horizontally from a 45-m high tower at 10 m/s. Its horizontal range when it strikes the ground is (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: From the previous problem, t = 3 s. Horizontal range R = u t = 10 × 3 = 30 m.

questions.question: At the highest point of a projectile launched at angle θ with speed u, the speed of the projectile is
questions.explanation: Vertical velocity vanishes at the apex; horizontal velocity u cos θ persists. So speed = |u cos θ|.

questions.question: A projectile is launched at speed u at 45°. The maximum height reached is
questions.explanation: H = u² sin² θ / (2g) = u² (1/2) / (2g) = u² / (4g).

questions.question: A football is kicked at 20 m/s at 45°. Its range on level ground is (g = 10 m/s²)
Which pair of launch angles will produce the same range on level ground (same speed)?
questions.explanation: Complementary angles (sum = 90°) give the same range. 20 + 70 = 90.

questions.question: In uniform circular motion, which of the following is constant?
questions.explanation: 'Uniform' here refers to constant speed. Velocity changes direction continuously, so it is not constant; nor is acceleration (it always points inward).

questions.question: The centripetal acceleration of a particle in uniform circular motion is directed
options: toward the centre of the circle
away from the centre of the circle
questions.answer: toward the centre of the circle
questions.explanation: Centripetal means 'centre-seeking'; the acceleration points perpendicular to the velocity, inward toward the centre.

questions.question: The centripetal acceleration of a particle moving at speed v in a circle of radius r is
questions.explanation: a_c = v² / r = ω² r, directed toward the centre.

questions.question: A particle moves in a circle of radius 2 m at constant speed 4 m/s. Its centripetal acceleration is
questions.explanation: a_c = v² / r = 16 / 2 = 8 m/s².

questions.question: A particle in uniform circular motion has angular speed ω = 4 rad/s and radius r = 0.5 m. Its centripetal acceleration is
The period T of a particle moving in a circle of radius r at speed v is
questions.explanation: Time for one revolution = circumference / speed = 2π r / v.

questions.question: A stone is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 1 m at 2 revolutions per second. Its centripetal acceleration is approximately
questions.explanation: ω = 2π × 2 = 4π rad/s; a_c = ω² r = (4π)² × 1 = 16π² m/s² ≈ 158 m/s².

questions.question: The centripetal force on a body of mass m moving at speed v in a circle of radius r is
questions.explanation: F_c = m × a_c = m v² / r, directed toward the centre.

questions.question: A car of mass 1000 kg is moving at 10 m/s around a curve of radius 50 m. The centripetal force required is
For a satellite in a circular orbit around Earth, the centripetal force is provided by
questions.explanation: Gravity supplies exactly the inward force needed to keep the satellite in its circular orbit.

questions.question: For a car taking a flat (un-banked) turn, the centripetal force is supplied by
options: friction between the tyres and the road
questions.answer: friction between the tyres and the road
questions.explanation: Static friction provides the inward force that turns the car. If the road is icy (no friction), the car cannot turn.

questions.question: A stone is whirled on a string in a horizontal circle. The centripetal force on the stone is provided by
questions.explanation: The string pulls the stone toward the centre with a force equal to the tension. Gravity acts vertically, not toward the centre of the horizontal circle.

questions.question: If the speed of a particle moving in a circle of fixed radius is doubled, the centripetal force becomes
questions.explanation: F_c = m v² / r, so F_c ∝ v². Doubling v multiplies F_c by 4.

questions.question: In uniform circular motion, the work done by the centripetal force in one complete revolution is
questions.explanation: Centripetal force is always perpendicular to velocity, so it does no work — W = F · d = F d cos 90° = 0 at every instant, and therefore zero over one revolution.

questions.question: If v_A and v_B are the velocities of two objects, the velocity of A relative to B is
questions.explanation: Relative velocity is a vector subtraction: v_AB = v_A − v_B.

questions.question: A boat can row at 5 m/s in still water. It heads straight across a river that flows at 3 m/s. The actual speed of the boat with respect to the bank is
questions.explanation: The boat's velocity components are 5 m/s across the river and 3 m/s downstream. Magnitude = √(5² + 3²) = √34 ≈ 5.83 m/s.

questions.question: A boat can row at 5 m/s in still water across a river 100 m wide flowing at 3 m/s. The minimum time to cross the river is
questions.explanation: Minimum time achieved by heading straight across; t = width / v_b = 100 / 5 = 20 s. (The river carries the boat downstream but does not affect across-stream speed.)

questions.question: A boat (still-water speed 5 m/s) wants to cross a river (current 3 m/s) along the shortest PATH. The boat must head upstream at an angle θ to the perpendicular such that sin θ equals
questions.explanation: For the resultant to be straight across, the upstream component must cancel the current: v_b sin θ = v_r, so sin θ = 3/5.

questions.question: If a river flows faster than the boat can row in still water (v_r > v_b), then the boat
options: can still cross straight across, just slowly
can never cross straight across — it must drift downstream
must travel along the bank first
questions.answer: can never cross straight across — it must drift downstream
questions.explanation: The required upstream cancellation is sin θ = v_r / v_b > 1, which is impossible. So the resultant must have a downstream component.

questions.question: Two cars approach an intersection from perpendicular roads, each at 30 km/h. The velocity of car A relative to car B has magnitude
questions.explanation: v_AB = v_A − v_B; the two velocity vectors are perpendicular and equal in magnitude, so |v_AB| = √(30² + 30²) = 30√2 km/h.

questions.question: Force is a scalar quantity.
questions.explanation: Force has both magnitude and direction, so it is a vector.

questions.question: Velocity is a vector, but speed is a scalar.
questions.explanation: Velocity carries direction; speed is just the magnitude.

questions.question: Two vectors of equal magnitude pointing in different directions are equal.
questions.explanation: Equality of vectors requires BOTH equal magnitude and equal direction.

questions.question: A vector can be slid parallel to itself in the plane without changing the vector.
questions.explanation: A vector is defined by magnitude and direction only; its location on the page is irrelevant.

questions.question: The resultant of two equal and opposite vectors is zero.
questions.explanation: A and (−A) sum to the zero vector.

questions.question: The resultant of two vectors of magnitudes 3 and 5 can have a magnitude of 1.
questions.explanation: The resultant lies between |5 − 3| = 2 and 5 + 3 = 8. So 1 is impossible.

questions.question: In 2D motion under constant acceleration, the horizontal and vertical motions are independent.
questions.explanation: Each component obeys the 1D kinematic equations independently — they share only the time t.

questions.question: The horizontal velocity of a projectile changes during its flight.
questions.explanation: No horizontal force acts, so a_x = 0 and v_x stays at u cos θ throughout.

questions.question: At the highest point of a projectile's trajectory, both the horizontal and the vertical velocity are zero.
questions.explanation: Only the vertical velocity is zero at the apex; the horizontal velocity u cos θ persists.

questions.question: The trajectory of a projectile launched at an angle is a parabola.
questions.explanation: y = x tan θ − g x² / (2 u² cos² θ) is quadratic in x — a parabola.

questions.question: On level ground, the range of a projectile is maximum at a launch angle of 45°.
questions.explanation: R = u² sin 2θ / g; the maximum of sin 2θ is at 2θ = 90°, i.e. θ = 45°.

questions.question: Two projectiles launched at the same speed at 30° and 60° have the same range and the same maximum height.
questions.explanation: They have the same range (complementary angles) but DIFFERENT maximum heights (the 60° projectile rises higher).

questions.question: In uniform circular motion, the speed is constant but the velocity changes.
questions.explanation: Speed is the magnitude of velocity; the direction of velocity changes continuously even though its magnitude is fixed.

questions.question: Centripetal acceleration points away from the centre of the circle.
questions.explanation: Centripetal means 'centre-seeking' — it points TOWARD the centre.

questions.question: The work done by the centripetal force on a particle in uniform circular motion over one full revolution is non-zero.
questions.explanation: Centripetal force is always perpendicular to velocity, so it does zero work at every instant — and therefore zero over any interval.

questions.question: Centripetal force is a new kind of force in addition to tension, gravity, friction etc.
questions.explanation: Centripetal force is the NET inward force required for circular motion — its physical origin can be tension, gravity, friction, normal force, etc. It is not a separate fundamental force.

questions.question: The outward push that a passenger feels in a turning car is caused by an outward centrifugal force in the ground frame.
questions.explanation: In the ground (inertial) frame there is no real outward force. The feeling arises because the passenger's body, by inertia, tends to continue in a straight line while the car turns inward.

questions.question: Relative velocity in 2D is computed by adding the velocities of the two objects.
questions.explanation: It is a vector SUBTRACTION: v_AB = v_A − v_B.

questions.question: If a river current is faster than the boat's still-water speed, the boat can never cross by the shortest path straight across.
questions.explanation: Crossing straight across requires sin θ = v_r / v_b. If v_r > v_b, sin θ > 1 — impossible. The boat must drift downstream.

questions.question: A quantity that has both magnitude and direction is called a ____.
questions.explanation: Vectors: displacement, velocity, force, etc. Scalars have only magnitude.

questions.question: The magnitude of a unit vector is ____.
questions.explanation: Unit vectors are defined to have magnitude exactly one.

questions.question: If a vector of magnitude A makes angle θ with the x-axis, its x-component is ____.
questions.explanation: By definition of resolution: A_x = A cos θ.

questions.question: If a vector of magnitude A makes angle θ with the x-axis, its y-component is ____.
questions.explanation: By definition of resolution: A_y = A sin θ.

questions.question: The magnitude of the resultant of two vectors A and B with angle θ between them is given by R² = ____.
questions.explanation: Cosine rule applied to the triangle of vectors.

questions.question: The time of flight of a projectile launched at speed u and angle θ on level ground is T = ____.
questions.explanation: Solve y = u sin θ · t − (1/2) g t² = 0 for t ≠ 0: t = 2 u sin θ / g.

questions.question: The maximum height of a projectile launched at speed u and angle θ is H = ____.
questions.explanation: Use v_y² = u_y² − 2 g H with v_y = 0 at apex: H = u_y² / (2g) = u² sin² θ / (2g).

questions.question: The range of a projectile launched at speed u and angle θ on level ground is R = ____.
questions.explanation: R = u cos θ × T = u cos θ × 2 u sin θ / g = u² × 2 sin θ cos θ / g = u² sin 2θ / g.

questions.question: The range of a projectile on level ground is maximum at a launch angle of ____.
questions.explanation: sin 2θ is maximum at 2θ = 90°, i.e. θ = 45°.

questions.question: The centripetal acceleration of a particle moving in a circle of radius r at speed v is a_c = ____.
questions.explanation: a_c = v² / r = ω² r, directed toward the centre.

questions.question: The centripetal force on a body of mass m moving at speed v in a circle of radius r is F_c = ____.
questions.explanation: F_c = m × a_c = m v² / r, directed toward the centre.

questions.question: The period of a particle moving in a circle of radius r at speed v is T = ____.
questions.explanation: Time for one complete revolution = circumference / speed.

questions.question: The velocity of A relative to B is v_AB = ____.
questions.explanation: Relative velocity is a vector subtraction.

questions.question: For a satellite in a circular orbit, the centripetal force is supplied by ____.
questions.explanation: Gravity provides exactly the inward force needed for circular orbit.

questions.question: For a car taking a flat (un-banked) turn, the centripetal force is supplied by ____.
questions.answer: friction between the tyres and the road
questions.explanation: Static friction supplies the inward force; on a frictionless road the car cannot turn.

questions.question: Distinguish a scalar from a vector quantity, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: A scalar is a physical quantity that is fully specified by a single number plus a unit; it has magnitude but no direction. Example: mass (3 kg). A vector quantity needs BOTH magnitude and direction to be fully specified. Example: velocity (10 m/s east).

questions.question: Under what condition are two vectors said to be equal? Does it matter where they are drawn on the page?
questions.answer: Two vectors are equal only when both their magnitudes and their directions agree. Where they are drawn does NOT matter — a vector is defined by magnitude and direction alone, so it can be slid parallel to itself anywhere on the page without changing it.

questions.question: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act at right angles on a body. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant.
questions.answer: Magnitude: R = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 N. Direction: tan α = 4/3 ⇒ α ≈ 53° from the 3-N force. So the resultant is 5 N at 53° from the 3-N direction.

questions.question: Find the resultant of two equal forces of magnitude 10 N each, when the angle between them is 60°.
questions.answer: R² = 10² + 10² + 2(10)(10) cos 60° = 100 + 100 + 200 × (1/2) = 300, so R = √300 = 10√3 ≈ 17.3 N. By symmetry the resultant bisects the angle between the two forces — it lies at 30° from either.

questions.question: Resolve a vector A = 50 N directed at 37° above the horizontal into its horizontal and vertical components.
questions.answer: A_x = A cos 37° = 50 × 0.8 = 40 N (horizontal). A_y = A sin 37° = 50 × 0.6 = 30 N (vertical). So A = 40 N î + 30 N ĵ.

questions.question: Given A = 3î + 4ĵ and B = 4î − 3ĵ, find A + B and its magnitude.
Explain why the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile can be treated independently.
questions.answer: Gravity acts only vertically. Therefore the horizontal component of acceleration is zero (a_x = 0) and the vertical component is constant (a_y = −g). Because the accelerations are independent and constant, each component obeys the 1D kinematic equations on its own. The two motions are linked only by the common time t — there is no x-y coupling in the equations.

questions.question: A projectile is launched at 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Find its time of flight, maximum height, and range. (g = 10 m/s²)
A stone is thrown horizontally from a 20-m high tower at 15 m/s. Find (i) the time to reach the ground and (ii) the horizontal distance from the foot of the tower where it lands. (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.answer: Vertical: free fall from rest, h = (1/2) g t² ⇒ 20 = 5 t² ⇒ t = 2 s. Horizontal: x = u t = 15 × 2 = 30 m. So the stone lands 30 m from the foot of the tower after 2 s.

questions.question: Show that the range of a projectile is the same for two launch angles θ and (90° − θ).
questions.answer: R(θ) = u² sin 2θ / g. R(90° − θ) = u² sin(180° − 2θ) / g = u² sin 2θ / g = R(θ). The two ranges are equal because sin 2(90° − θ) = sin(180° − 2θ) = sin 2θ. Although the ranges are equal, the maximum heights and times of flight differ (the larger angle gives a higher, slower flight).

questions.question: Explain why uniform circular motion is accelerated motion, even though the speed is constant.
questions.answer: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, NOT of speed. In uniform circular motion the direction of velocity changes continuously while its magnitude (speed) stays constant. Because the velocity vector is changing, there is a non-zero acceleration — the centripetal acceleration — directed toward the centre of the circle.

questions.question: A car moves at 20 m/s around a circular track of radius 50 m. Find its centripetal acceleration.
questions.answer: a_c = v² / r = 20² / 50 = 400 / 50 = 8 m/s², directed toward the centre of the track.

questions.question: A 0.5-kg stone is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 1 m at a speed of 4 m/s. Find the tension in the string.
questions.answer: The tension supplies the centripetal force. F_c = m v² / r = 0.5 × 16 / 1 = 8 N. So the tension in the string is 8 N. (We ignore the weight here because the circle is horizontal and we ask only for the centripetal component.)

questions.question: Is the centripetal force a new kind of force in physics? Explain.
questions.answer: No. 'Centripetal force' is just a label for the NET inward force required to keep a body in circular motion. Its physical origin varies with the situation: tension (whirled stone), friction (turning car), gravity (orbiting satellite), normal force (ball on a banked track), or some combination of these.

questions.question: A boat with still-water speed 4 m/s heads straight across a river that flows at 3 m/s. Find the magnitude and direction of the boat's actual velocity relative to the bank.
questions.answer: Components: 4 m/s across-stream and 3 m/s downstream. Magnitude = √(4² + 3²) = 5 m/s. Direction: tan α = 3/4 ⇒ α ≈ 37° from the perpendicular to the bank (i.e. 37° downstream from straight-across).

questions.question: A river 200 m wide flows at 2 m/s. A boat can move at 5 m/s in still water. (i) What is the minimum time to cross? (ii) How far downstream does the boat land if it heads straight across?
questions.answer: (i) Minimum time = width / boat speed across = 200 / 5 = 40 s (achieved by heading straight across). (ii) Drift = river speed × time = 2 × 40 = 80 m downstream from the directly-opposite point.

questions.question: A boat with still-water speed 5 m/s needs to cross a 100-m wide river that flows at 3 m/s along the shortest PATH. Find the heading angle (from the perpendicular) and the time taken to cross.
questions.answer: For shortest path the resultant must be perpendicular to the bank, so the upstream component of the boat's velocity must cancel the current: 5 sin θ = 3 ⇒ sin θ = 3/5 ⇒ θ = 37°. Across-stream component = 5 cos 37° = 5 × 0.8 = 4 m/s. Time = width / across-stream speed = 100 / 4 = 25 s.

questions.question: Two vectors A and B have magnitudes 6 and 8. The resultant has magnitude 10. Find the angle between A and B.
questions.answer: R² = A² + B² + 2AB cos θ ⇒ 100 = 36 + 64 + 96 cos θ = 100 + 96 cos θ ⇒ cos θ = 0 ⇒ θ = 90°. The vectors are perpendicular.

questions.question: A projectile is launched from the ground at 50 m/s at 53° above the horizontal. Find the position (x, y) at t = 4 s. (g = 10 m/s², sin 53° = 0.8, cos 53° = 0.6)
A satellite orbits Earth at a speed of 7.8 km/s in a circular orbit of radius 6.7 × 10⁶ m. Find its centripetal acceleration.
questions.answer: v = 7800 m/s. a_c = v² / r = (7800)² / (6.7 × 10⁶) = 6.084 × 10⁷ / 6.7 × 10⁶ ≈ 9.08 m/s². (This matches the local value of g at that altitude, as expected — gravity supplies the centripetal force.)

questions.question: State and explain the parallelogram law of vector addition. Derive the expression for the magnitude and direction of the resultant of two vectors A and B inclined at angle θ to each other.
questions.answer:
Parallelogram law: If two vectors are represented in magnitude and direction by the two adjacent sides of a parallelogram drawn from a common point, then their resultant is represented by the diagonal of the parallelogram drawn from the same point.

Derivation: Let OA = A and OB = B with angle θ between them. Complete the parallelogram OACB. The diagonal OC = R = A + B. Drop a perpendicular from C to OA extended, meeting it at D. Then AD = B cos θ and CD = B sin θ.

In the right triangle OCD: OC² = OD² + CD² = (OA + AD)² + CD² = (A + B cos θ)² + (B sin θ)². Expanding: R² = A² + 2AB cos θ + B² cos² θ + B² sin² θ = A² + B² + 2AB cos θ (using sin² θ + cos² θ = 1).

Direction: If R makes angle α with A, then tan α = CD / OD = (B sin θ) / (A + B cos θ).

Limiting cases: θ = 0° gives R = A + B (parallel); θ = 180° gives R = |A − B| (anti-parallel); θ = 90° gives R = √(A² + B²).

questions.question: A particle is projected with speed u at an angle θ above the horizontal from level ground. Derive expressions for (a) the time of flight, (b) the maximum height, (c) the horizontal range, and (d) the equation of trajectory.
questions.answer:
Take launch point as origin, x-axis horizontal in direction of motion, y-axis vertical upward. Initial components: u_x = u cos θ, u_y = u sin θ. Accelerations: a_x = 0, a_y = −g. Therefore at time t: x = u cos θ · t and y = u sin θ · t − (1/2) g t².

(a) Time of flight T: set y = 0 (projectile returns to launch height): u sin θ · t − (1/2) g t² = 0 ⇒ t [u sin θ − (1/2) g t] = 0. Non-trivial root: T = 2 u sin θ / g.

(b) Maximum height H: at apex v_y = 0. Use v_y² = u_y² − 2 g H ⇒ H = u_y² / (2g) = u² sin² θ / (2g). (Alternatively: at apex t = T/2 = u sin θ / g, then H = u sin θ × T/2 − (1/2) g (T/2)² gives the same result.)

(c) Range R: R = u_x × T = u cos θ × 2 u sin θ / g = 2 u² sin θ cos θ / g = u² sin 2θ / g.

(d) Trajectory: from x = u cos θ · t, t = x / (u cos θ). Substitute into y: y = u sin θ × (x / u cos θ) − (1/2) g × (x / u cos θ)² = x tan θ − g x² / (2 u² cos² θ). This is the equation of a parabola opening downward.

questions.question: (a) Show that the horizontal range of a projectile on level ground is maximum at a launch angle of 45°. (b) Two projectiles are launched at the same speed at 30° and 60°. Compare their ranges, times of flight, and maximum heights.
questions.answer:
(a) R(θ) = u² sin 2θ / g. dR/dθ = (2 u² / g) cos 2θ. Set to zero: cos 2θ = 0 ⇒ 2θ = 90° ⇒ θ = 45°. The second derivative is negative there, so this is a maximum. R_max = u² / g.

(b) Range: R(30°) = u² sin 60° / g = (u²√3) / (2g). R(60°) = u² sin 120° / g = (u²√3) / (2g). EQUAL (as expected for complementary angles, since sin 60° = sin 120°).

Time of flight: T = 2 u sin θ / g. T(30°) = u / g; T(60°) = u√3 / g. So the 60° projectile takes √3 times as long — it spends longer in flight.

Maximum height: H = u² sin² θ / (2g). H(30°) = u² × (1/4) / (2g) = u² / (8g). H(60°) = u² × (3/4) / (2g) = 3 u² / (8g). So the 60° projectile rises three times higher than the 30° one. The two projectiles trace very different parabolas yet land at the same horizontal distance.

questions.question: Derive an expression for the centripetal acceleration of a particle moving in a circle of radius r at constant speed v. State its direction and explain why uniform circular motion is accelerated motion.
questions.answer:
Consider a particle moving on a circle of radius r at speed v. At time t it is at A with velocity v_A; a short time Δt later at B with velocity v_B. Both velocity vectors have the same magnitude v but their directions differ by the small angle Δθ that the position vector has swept through. The arc length AB = v Δt, so Δθ = v Δt / r (radians).

Draw v_A and v_B from a common point. The change Δv = v_B − v_A is a vector connecting the tip of v_A to the tip of v_B. For small Δθ, |Δv| ≈ v Δθ (chord of a small angle on a circle of radius v). So |Δv| = v × (v Δt / r) = v² Δt / r.

Magnitude of acceleration: a = |Δv| / Δt = v² / r. As Δt → 0, the direction of Δv becomes perpendicular to v_A and points toward the centre of the circle. Therefore a_c = v² / r, directed toward the centre. Using v = ω r, we can also write a_c = ω² r.

Why it is accelerated motion: acceleration is the rate of change of velocity (a vector), not speed (a scalar). In uniform circular motion the magnitude of velocity is constant but its direction changes continuously, so the velocity vector is changing — and the rate of that change is the centripetal acceleration v² / r.

questions.question: A car of mass 1200 kg goes around an unbanked circular track of radius 80 m at a speed of 20 m/s. (a) Find the centripetal acceleration. (b) Find the required centripetal force. (c) If the coefficient of friction between the tyres and the road is 0.4, can the car make the turn safely? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.answer:
(a) a_c = v² / r = 400 / 80 = 5 m/s² directed toward the centre of the track.

(b) Required centripetal force F_c = m a_c = 1200 × 5 = 6000 N. This force must be supplied by friction between the tyres and the road.

(c) Maximum available friction: f_max = μ × N = μ × m g = 0.4 × 1200 × 10 = 4800 N. Required force is 6000 N. Since required (6000 N) > available (4800 N), the friction is insufficient and the car will skid outward (i.e. fail to make the turn at this speed).

Maximum safe speed: v_max = √(μ g r) = √(0.4 × 10 × 80) = √320 ≈ 17.9 m/s. To make the turn safely the driver must slow down to below ~18 m/s, or the road must be banked.

questions.question: Discuss the river-crossing problem. A boat can move at speed v_b in still water; a river of width d flows with speed v_r. (a) For the boat to cross straight across (shortest path), find the angle the boat must make with the perpendicular and the time taken. (b) For the shortest time of crossing, what heading should the boat take, and what is the time and the downstream drift?
questions.answer:
(a) Shortest path: the resultant velocity (boat + river) must be perpendicular to the bank. The boat must head partly upstream so that its upstream component v_b sin θ cancels the river's drag v_r:
   v_b sin θ = v_r ⇒ sin θ = v_r / v_b.
This is only possible if v_b > v_r (else sin θ > 1). The across-stream component of the boat's velocity is v_b cos θ = √(v_b² − v_r²). Time to cross: t_path = d / √(v_b² − v_r²). The boat travels in a straight line directly across the river but takes longer.

(b) Shortest time: the boat heads STRAIGHT across (θ = 0 from the perpendicular). The full v_b goes into crossing, so across-stream speed = v_b. Time: t_min = d / v_b. The river simultaneously carries the boat downstream with speed v_r, so downstream drift = v_r × t_min = v_r d / v_b. The boat lands downstream of the directly-opposite point.

Comparison: t_min = d / v_b < d / √(v_b² − v_r²) = t_path, so heading straight across is always quicker — but at the cost of a downstream drift, and a longer total path travelled relative to the water.

questions.question: Three vectors A = 5î + 2ĵ, B = 3î − 4ĵ and C = −2î + 6ĵ act at a point. Find the resultant vector and its magnitude. Determine the angle it makes with the positive x-axis.
questions.answer:
Sum the components:
x: 5 + 3 + (−2) = 6
y: 2 + (−4) + 6 = 4
Resultant R = 6î + 4ĵ.

Magnitude: |R| = √(6² + 4²) = √(36 + 16) = √52 = 2√13 ≈ 7.21.

Angle with the positive x-axis: tan α = 4/6 = 2/3 ⇒ α = arctan(2/3) ≈ 33.7°. Since both components are positive, the resultant lies in the first quadrant.

questions.question: A ball is projected horizontally with speed 10 m/s from the top of a tower 80 m high. Find (a) the time taken to reach the ground, (b) the horizontal distance from the foot of the tower at which it strikes the ground, (c) the velocity (magnitude and direction) with which it strikes the ground. (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.answer:
(a) Vertical motion: free fall from rest, h = (1/2) g t². So 80 = 5 t² ⇒ t² = 16 ⇒ t = 4 s.

(b) Horizontal motion: x = u_x t = 10 × 4 = 40 m. So the ball lands 40 m from the foot of the tower.

(c) Velocity at impact: v_x = 10 m/s (unchanged); v_y = g t = 10 × 4 = 40 m/s downward. Magnitude: v = √(10² + 40²) = √(100 + 1600) = √1700 = 10√17 ≈ 41.2 m/s. Direction: tan φ = v_y / v_x = 40/10 = 4 ⇒ φ ≈ 76° below the horizontal.

questions.question: A particle moves in a circle of radius 0.5 m at a constant angular speed of 10 rad/s. Find (a) its linear speed, (b) its centripetal acceleration, (c) the time taken for one complete revolution, and (d) the frequency of revolution.
questions.answer:
(a) v = ω r = 10 × 0.5 = 5 m/s.
(b) a_c = ω² r = 100 × 0.5 = 50 m/s² (or equivalently v²/r = 25/0.5 = 50 m/s²).
(c) T = 2π / ω = 2π / 10 = π/5 s ≈ 0.628 s.
(d) f = 1/T = 10 / (2π) = 5/π Hz ≈ 1.59 Hz (revolutions per second).

questions.question: Justify the assumptions implicit in the standard projectile-motion formulas T = 2u sinθ/g, H = u²sin²θ/(2g), R = u²sin2θ/g. Discuss how each formula must be modified or treated if (i) the projectile lands at a different height from the launch point, (ii) air resistance is significant, (iii) the projectile travels long distances over a curved Earth.
questions.answer:
Implicit assumptions: (1) acceleration due to gravity is constant in magnitude and direction throughout the flight, (2) air resistance is neglected, (3) the projectile lands at the same height as the launch point, (4) Earth is flat (no curvature) and non-rotating over the timescale of the flight.

(i) Different launch and landing heights: the time-of-flight equation u sinθ·t − (1/2)g t² = 0 no longer applies. Instead solve u sinθ·t − (1/2)g t² = y_landing for t (a quadratic with one positive root). The range R = u cosθ × t with this new t. The 45° optimum no longer holds — for a launch from a height the optimum angle is less than 45°; for landing at a higher point it is more than 45°.

(ii) Air resistance: the standard formulas FAIL completely. With drag, the trajectory is no longer a parabola; the projectile decelerates horizontally, descends faster on the down-leg than the up-leg, and the range, height and time are all reduced. The motion is no longer separable into independent x- and y-components because drag depends on the SPEED (combined components).

(iii) Long distances over curved Earth: gravity no longer points in a fixed direction (it points toward Earth's centre). For distances larger than a few hundred km the parabolic approximation must be replaced by an ellipse (Kepler orbit). For a flat-Earth approximation to be reasonable, the range R must be much smaller than the Earth's radius (~6400 km).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A fielder kicks a football from level ground at a speed of 20 m/s at an angle of 60° above the horizontal. The ball clears the head of an opponent standing 30 m away. Take g = 10 m/s².

(i) What are the initial horizontal and vertical components of the ball's velocity?
(ii) Find the time the ball takes to reach the opponent's position (x = 30 m).
(iii) At what height does the ball pass over the opponent?
(iv) What is the maximum height reached by the ball?
questions.answer:
(i) u_x = u cos 60° = 20 × 0.5 = 10 m/s. u_y = u sin 60° = 20 × (√3/2) = 10√3 m/s ≈ 17.32 m/s.
(ii) t = x / u_x = 30 / 10 = 3 s.
(iii) y = u_y t − (1/2) g t² = 10√3 × 3 − 5 × 9 = 30√3 − 45 ≈ 51.96 − 45 ≈ 6.96 m. So the ball passes about 7 m above the opponent's feet.
(iv) H = u² sin² 60° / (2g) = 400 × 0.75 / 20 = 15 m.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A cricket coach is comparing two batsmen. Both hit the ball at the same speed of 30 m/s but at different launch angles: batsman A at 30° and batsman B at 60°. The ground is level. Take g = 10 m/s².

(i) Find the range achieved by each batsman.
(ii) Find the maximum height reached by each shot.
(iii) Find the time of flight in each case.
(iv) Which batsman's shot stays in the air longer, and why?
questions.answer:
(i) Range: R = u² sin 2θ / g = 900/10 × sin 2θ = 90 sin 2θ. R(30°) = 90 sin 60° = 45√3 ≈ 77.9 m. R(60°) = 90 sin 120° = 45√3 ≈ 77.9 m. EQUAL — complementary angles give the same range.
(ii) H = u² sin² θ / (2g) = 45 sin² θ. H(30°) = 45 × 0.25 = 11.25 m. H(60°) = 45 × 0.75 = 33.75 m. Batsman B's shot rises three times higher.
(iii) T = 2u sin θ / g = 6 sin θ. T(30°) = 3 s; T(60°) = 3√3 ≈ 5.2 s.
(iv) Batsman B's shot stays airborne longer (5.2 s vs 3 s) because its larger vertical component (u sin 60° > u sin 30°) means more time spent rising and falling, even though both shots cover the same horizontal distance. A fielder thus has more time to position themselves under a high lofted shot.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A child sits 4 m from the centre of a merry-go-round that completes one full revolution every 8 seconds. The child has mass 30 kg.

(i) What is the angular speed ω of the merry-go-round?
(ii) What is the linear speed v of the child?
(iii) What is the centripetal acceleration of the child?
(iv) What centripetal force is required to keep the child moving in a circle, and what physical agent supplies it?
questions.answer:
(i) ω = 2π / T = 2π / 8 = π/4 rad/s ≈ 0.785 rad/s.
(ii) v = ω r = (π/4) × 4 = π m/s ≈ 3.14 m/s.
(iii) a_c = v² / r = π² / 4 ≈ 2.47 m/s² (or equivalently ω² r = (π/4)² × 4 = π²/4).
(iv) F_c = m a_c = 30 × π²/4 ≈ 74 N, directed toward the centre. The force is supplied by the seat / safety bar / floor friction on the child — whatever physical contact pushes the child inward toward the axis.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A car of mass 1000 kg negotiates an un-banked (flat) circular curve of radius 50 m at a speed of 15 m/s. The coefficient of friction between the tyres and the road is 0.5. Take g = 10 m/s².

(i) What centripetal force is required for the car to make this turn?
(ii) What is the maximum friction force the road can supply?
(iii) Can the car make the turn safely? Explain.
(iv) What is the maximum safe speed on this curve?
questions.answer:
(i) F_c = m v² / r = 1000 × 225 / 50 = 4500 N, directed toward the centre.
(ii) f_max = μ m g = 0.5 × 1000 × 10 = 5000 N.
(iii) Yes. Required force (4500 N) is less than available friction (5000 N), so the tyres can supply the inward force without skidding.
(iv) v_max occurs when f_max = m v_max² / r ⇒ v_max = √(μ g r) = √(0.5 × 10 × 50) = √250 ≈ 15.8 m/s. The driver is currently going at 15 m/s, just below the safe limit.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A river is 120 m wide and flows at 4 m/s. A boatman has a boat that can move at 5 m/s in still water. He wants to deliver a parcel to a point directly across the river.

(i) If the boatman heads straight across, how long does the boat take to cross? How far downstream does it land?
(ii) To land directly opposite, what angle must the boatman make with the perpendicular to the bank?
(iii) How long does the boat take to cross by the shortest-path route?
(iv) Compare the two strategies: which is faster and which is straighter, and why?
questions.answer:
(i) Heading straight across: across-stream speed = 5 m/s, t = 120 / 5 = 24 s. Downstream drift = 4 × 24 = 96 m.
(ii) For shortest path (directly opposite), the boatman must head upstream so the upstream component cancels the river: 5 sin θ = 4 ⇒ sin θ = 4/5 ⇒ θ = 53° from the perpendicular (i.e. 37° from straight across).
(iii) Across-stream component = 5 cos 53° = 5 × 0.6 = 3 m/s. Time = 120 / 3 = 40 s.
(iv) Heading straight across is FASTER (24 s vs 40 s) but the boat lands 96 m downstream. Heading partly upstream lands the boat directly opposite (zero drift) but takes longer because part of the boat's velocity is spent fighting the current. The boatman chooses based on whether time or location matters more.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A boat is being pulled along a canal by two horses on opposite banks. Each horse pulls with a force of 1000 N. The ropes from the two horses make angles of 30° with the boat's direction of motion (one on each side).

(i) Resolve each horse's pull into components along and perpendicular to the boat's direction of motion.
(ii) Find the net force along the direction of motion.
(iii) Find the net force perpendicular to the direction of motion.
(iv) What is the magnitude and direction of the resultant force on the boat?
questions.answer:
(i) For each horse: component along the direction of motion = 1000 × cos 30° = 500√3 ≈ 866 N (forward); component perpendicular = 1000 × sin 30° = 500 N (toward the bank that horse is on).
(ii) Net forward force = 2 × 500√3 = 1000√3 ≈ 1732 N.
(iii) The two perpendicular components are equal and opposite (one toward each bank), so they cancel. Net perpendicular force = 0.
(iv) Resultant = 1000√3 N ≈ 1732 N, directed along the boat's direction of motion. By symmetry the side pulls cancel and only the forward components add.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A stone is thrown from the top of a cliff 45 m high. The initial speed is 20 m/s and the launch direction is 30° ABOVE the horizontal. Take g = 10 m/s².

(i) Find the maximum height (above the cliff top) that the stone reaches.
(ii) Find the total time the stone is in the air, from launch to landing on the ground at the foot of the cliff.
(iii) Find the horizontal range from the foot of the cliff at which the stone lands.
(iv) Why doesn't the standard formula R = u² sin 2θ / g give the right range here?
questions.answer:
(i) u_y = 20 sin 30° = 10 m/s. H_above_cliff = u_y² / (2g) = 100 / 20 = 5 m. Maximum height above ground = 45 + 5 = 50 m.
(ii) y(t) = u_y t − (1/2) g t², measured from cliff top with positive upward. Landing when y = −45 (45 m below cliff top): 10 t − 5 t² = −45, so 5 t² − 10 t − 45 = 0, t² − 2 t − 9 = 0, t = (2 + √(4 + 36)) / 2 = 1 + √10 ≈ 4.16 s.
(iii) u_x = 20 cos 30° = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m/s. Range = u_x × t = 17.32 × 4.16 ≈ 72 m from the foot of the cliff.
(iv) The formula R = u² sin 2θ / g assumes the projectile returns to its launch HEIGHT. Here the launch is 45 m above the landing point, so the time of flight is longer than 2 u sin θ / g and the actual range is larger than that the formula predicts.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A particle is acted on by three coplanar forces: F₁ = 6 N along the positive x-axis, F₂ = 8 N along the positive y-axis, and F₃ = 5 N along the direction making 53° with the positive x-axis. (sin 53° = 0.8, cos 53° = 0.6)

(i) Resolve F₃ into x- and y-components.
(ii) Find the net force on the particle in component form.
(iii) Find the magnitude of the net force.
(iv) Find the angle the net force makes with the positive x-axis.
questions.answer:
(i) F₃_x = 5 cos 53° = 5 × 0.6 = 3 N. F₃_y = 5 sin 53° = 5 × 0.8 = 4 N.
(ii) F_net_x = 6 + 0 + 3 = 9 N. F_net_y = 0 + 8 + 4 = 12 N. So F_net = 9î + 12ĵ N.
(iii) |F_net| = √(9² + 12²) = √(81 + 144) = √225 = 15 N.
(iv) tan α = 12/9 = 4/3, so α = arctan(4/3) ≈ 53° from the positive x-axis. Both components are positive, so it lies in the first quadrant.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

The International Space Station (ISS) orbits Earth at an altitude of about 400 km above Earth's surface. Earth's radius is approximately 6400 km. At this altitude, g ≈ 8.7 m/s². The ISS moves in (approximately) uniform circular motion.

(i) What provides the centripetal force on the ISS?
(ii) Find the orbital radius r (distance from Earth's centre).
(iii) Find the orbital speed v needed to keep the ISS in this circular orbit.
(iv) Find the orbital period T (time for one complete revolution around Earth). Express T in minutes.
questions.answer:
(i) Earth's gravitational attraction — there is nothing else acting on the ISS at this altitude.
(ii) r = R_Earth + altitude = 6400 + 400 = 6800 km = 6.8 × 10⁶ m.
(iii) Centripetal acceleration must equal gravity: v² / r = g_400 ⇒ v = √(g × r) = √(8.7 × 6.8 × 10⁶) = √(5.916 × 10⁷) ≈ 7690 m/s ≈ 7.7 km/s.
(iv) T = 2π r / v = (2π × 6.8 × 10⁶) / 7690 ≈ 5555 s ≈ 92.6 minutes. The ISS thus completes about 16 orbits per day.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A pilot wants to fly her aeroplane due NORTH at a ground speed of 200 km/h. There is a wind blowing from the WEST at 50 km/h.

(i) Sketch (in words) the relationship between the plane's velocity through the air, the wind's velocity, and the plane's velocity over the ground.
(ii) In what direction (relative to north) must the pilot head the plane?
(iii) What airspeed (speed relative to the air) must the pilot maintain to achieve a ground speed of 200 km/h due north?
(iv) What practical lesson does this carry for pilots flying in cross-winds?
questions.answer:
(i) The velocity of the plane relative to the ground equals the velocity of the plane relative to the air PLUS the velocity of the air relative to the ground (the wind). To make the ground velocity point due north when the wind blows east, the airspeed vector must have a westward component cancelling the wind's eastward push.
(ii) The pilot must 'crab' into the wind — heading the nose of the plane slightly west of north. The west-component of the airspeed must equal 50 km/h (cancelling the eastward wind). If airspeed magnitude is V then V sin θ = 50, where θ is the angle west of north.
(iii) To go 200 km/h north over ground, the north component of airspeed must be 200 km/h. So V cos θ = 200 and V sin θ = 50. Therefore V = √(200² + 50²) = √(42500) ≈ 206 km/h. The crab angle is θ = arctan(50/200) ≈ 14° west of north.
(iv) Pilots must continuously adjust heading to compensate for cross-winds; ignoring the wind will cause the plane to drift sideways off the planned track. Modern aircraft use this 'crab angle' technique routinely during cross-wind landings and en-route navigation.
